name: Minoxidil + finasteride stack
lead: The minoxidil plus finasteride stack, often abbreviated "fin+min" on forums, is the combined use of minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, and finasteride, which lowers dihydrotestosterone (DHT), to keep and thicken hair in male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia). Hair density and hairline are among the most visible parts of a person's appearance, and the pairing is the baseline hair-loss regimen discussed in looksmaxxing communities: finasteride aims to slow the miniaturisation of follicles, and minoxidil aims to regrow and thicken hair in affected areas.[1][2][4]

Topical minoxidil was approved by the US FDA for male baldness in August 1988 as Rogaine, and finasteride 1 mg for male pattern hair loss in 1997 as Propecia.[3][4] A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found 5% minoxidil, 2% minoxidil, 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser therapy each superior to placebo for hair growth in men.[2] The two drugs act by different mechanisms, which is the usual reason given for combining them; dermatologists quoted by NBC News said finasteride mainly prevents further loss and is usually combined with topical minoxidil for regrowth.[13]

Finasteride carries documented sexual, mood and other adverse effects whose persistence after stopping is contested, and in May 2025 the European Medicines Agency's safety committee confirmed suicidal ideation as a side effect, with a patient card added to finasteride 1 mg packs.[4][14] Minoxidil's effects are reversible: hair gained is generally lost again within months after stopping.[3]

chain: Finasteride lowers DHT, the hormone that miniaturises susceptible follicles
Minoxidil prolongs follicle growth and thickens hair
Hairline and density are kept longer and partly regained
angle.text: Users take the two drugs together so that finasteride slows ongoing loss while minoxidil adds regrowth, aiming for a fuller hairline and crown. Both are FDA-approved for male pattern hair loss, and the benefit lasts while treatment continues.

paras: Pattern hair loss is common: Wikipedia reports that about half of men have it by age 50, and that it is believed to result from genetics combined with DHT. Minoxidil, finasteride and dutasteride are the drugs with evidence in male pattern loss, and Wikipedia notes they typically work better to prevent further loss than to regrow lost hair.[16]

In practice, the stack is described as a retention-and-regrowth routine. Finasteride is taken by mouth as a daily tablet (a topical form is used by some), and minoxidil is applied to the scalp as a solution or foam, or taken by mouth off-label in low doses. NBC News quoted dermatologists saying that starting earlier gives better results, that finasteride is prescribed constantly, and that it is typically combined with topical minoxidil for regrowth.[13] Because both effects depend on continued use, the stack is a long-term routine; minoxidil gains disappear after stopping, and Wikipedia reports that almost all topical users stop within a year.[3]

Within looksmaxxing, fin+min is treated as the foundation for anyone with a receding hairline or thinning crown, usually before considering hair transplants or other procedures. Forum replies also mention alternatives such as rosemary oil,[17] and one meta-analysis found low-level laser therapy superior to placebo in men.[2]

Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn in the 1960s as an anti-ulcer candidate that turned out to be a strong vasodilator. Wikipedia reports it was named in 1963, introduced in 1971 for severe high blood pressure, and approved as oral tablets (Loniten) in 1979, with researchers noticing hair growth as a side effect. The FDA approved it for male baldness as Rogaine in August 1988; a 1996 decision allowed over-the-counter sale and generics.[3]

Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by the follicular enzyme sulfotransferase into minoxidil sulfate, a potassium channel opener. A 2022 review describes its action as involving several pathways, including vasodilation, anti-inflammatory effects and the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway, and says it may lengthen the growth phase of the hair cycle; the review adds that people with higher sulfotransferase activity may respond better.[5] Topical use is available as 2% and 5% solutions and 5% foam; about 1.4% is absorbed through the skin.[5][3]

Finasteride was developed by Merck as MK-906. Wikipedia traces the idea to 1974 reports of 5-alpha-reductase deficiency in children in the Caribbean, who as adults had little male pattern baldness, and to a 1975 effort led by Merck research head P. Roy Vagelos to mimic the condition to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia. It was patented in 1984, approved in 1992 at the 5 mg strength for BPH (Proscar), and in 1997 at the 1 mg strength for male pattern hair loss (Propecia).[4]

It inhibits the type II and III isoforms of 5-alpha-reductase, lowering serum DHT by about 70 percent and scalp DHT by 65 to 70 percent, but has weak action against type I and so does not fully suppress DHT, unlike dutasteride.[4] It also reduces neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, which Wikipedia links to proposed effects on mood and sexual function.[4] Merck's hair-loss patent expired in November 2013, after which generic finasteride became widely available.[4]

subs.h: Related drugs: dutasteride and oral minoxidil
paras: A 2022 review comparing oral minoxidil, finasteride and dutasteride gave a probable efficacy ranking in decreasing order of dutasteride, higher-strength finasteride, oral minoxidil, standard-strength finasteride and then very low-dose oral minoxidil. It noted that oral dutasteride and oral minoxidil are used off-label, and that Japan and South Korea have approved dutasteride for male pattern hair loss.[1]

Low-dose oral minoxidil emerged for hair loss around 2015, involving work by Rodney Sinclair and others, and Wikipedia says interest rose sharply after a New York Times article in August 2022.[3] A 2021 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology covers its efficacy and safety.[20] Oral minoxidil is discussed in forums as an alternative for people who dislike scalp application or who want to avoid finasteride.

The 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology analysed separate groups of trials and found 5% minoxidil, 2% minoxidil, 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser light therapy in men, and 2% minoxidil in women, each superior to placebo.[2] A 48-week randomised trial in men found 5% minoxidil gave significantly greater improvement in non-vellus hair count and in patient and investigator ratings of scalp coverage than 2% minoxidil or placebo, with about 45 percent more regrowth than 2% at week 48; itching and local irritation were more frequent with 5%.[7]

For finasteride, Wikipedia reports two meta-analyses finding about 15 percent regrowth, with greatest effect at the crown, and notes that it works less well in women with pattern hair loss.[4] NBC News quoted dermatologist Jerry Shapiro estimating an 80 to 90 percent chance of preventing further loss, and described a Korean five-year study in which nearly all men kept or gained hair and an Italian study in which 86 percent had no change after ten years.[13]

A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies concluded that many over-the-counter, prescription and procedural treatments promote hair growth, and highlighted the benefit of a multifaceted, individualised approach.[9] A 2023 review in Drugs describes the condition as chronic and notes that only topical minoxidil and oral finasteride are FDA-approved for it.[12]

Most randomised evidence is on single agents. A 2024 double-blind randomised trial in JAMA Dermatology enrolled 90 men and compared daily oral minoxidil with twice-daily 5% topical minoxidil over 24 weeks; 68 completed it. Hair density differences were not statistically significant, photographic analysis favoured oral minoxidil on the vertex but not the front, and hypertrichosis occurred in 22 of 45 (49 percent) of the oral group. The authors concluded oral minoxidil did not demonstrate superiority over the topical form.[6] A 2022 review had earlier concluded that oral minoxidil was more effective than topical 5% and 2% after six months in male pattern loss.[5]

Combination-specific studies are fewer and smaller. A retrospective Indian study of 50 men aged 20 to 40 followed those who had two years of topical minoxidil plus oral finasteride and then switched to 5% minoxidil fortified with 0.1% finasteride topically; about 84 percent of the 45 who continued maintained good hair density, and four of five who had stopped and then restarted improved.[8] Registered trials include a completed phase 3 trial of combined minoxidil and finasteride lotion versus minoxidil lotion (NCT01391156, 40 participants) and a 2023 phase 2/3 trial of topical finasteride plus minoxidil against topical minoxidil (NCT05990400, 40 participants).[10][11]

Other studies have tested add-ons: one examined low-level laser therapy alone or together with minoxidil or finasteride,[21] and a 2024 randomised trial compared topical minoxidil combined with oral spironolactone against topical minoxidil combined with oral finasteride in people with pattern hair loss.[22]

Wikipedia reports reduced libido, erectile dysfunction and lower semen volume as the most common effects in men treated for hair loss, gynecomastia in about 1.5 percent, and reports of depression and suicidality. A 2017 review of nearly 12,000 patients found 1.4 percent had erectile dysfunction lasting at least 90 days after stopping.[4] NBC News quoted doctors putting common sexual side effects under 5 percent of men, and dermatologist Jerry Shapiro calling the risk of permanent side effects very rare, while dermatologist Maria Colavincenzo said she is cautious in patients who already have sexual function problems.[13]

Post-finasteride syndrome, a proposed condition of persistent sexual, neurological and psychological symptoms after stopping, is disputed. A 2019 BMJ editorial called it ill defined and controversial, and a meta-analysis found associations with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction after discontinuation but with limited evidence quality.[4] The FDA updated the label in 2012 to describe persistent sexual effects, and NBC News reports a 2022 label warning about possible suicidal behaviour.[4][13] Merck faced about 1,370 product-liability suits and settled most by 2018.[4] The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy, and the FDA advises deferring blood donation for a month after the last dose.[4]

Topical minoxidil commonly causes itching, irritation, dryness and contact dermatitis, often linked to alcohol or propylene glycol in the vehicle.[3] Oral minoxidil at blood-pressure doses can cause fluid retention, rapid heartbeat and pericardial effusion, and at low doses for hair loss the most common effect is hypertrichosis, with headaches and cardiovascular symptoms reported.[3][1][6] Minoxidil is highly toxic to cats and dogs, according to Wikipedia.[3]

In May 2025 the European Medicines Agency's pharmacovigilance committee confirmed suicidal ideation as a side effect of finasteride 1 mg and 5 mg tablets, frequency unknown, while concluding that benefits continue to outweigh risks for approved uses. It found no established link for dutasteride, added mood-change wording to its information as a precaution, and found no evidence linking suicidal ideation to finasteride skin sprays. A patient card is to be included in the 1 mg pack.[14]

The UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency issued a 2024 alert that finasteride has been associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction, according to an advocacy group's summary of a BBC Radio 4 File on 4 investigation broadcast in January 2026. That investigation reported that TikTok removed content and banned three accounts of influencers promoting finasteride with discount codes after reporters passed the posts to the regulator.[15]

sections.h: Spread online and in looksmaxxing culture
paras: NBC News reported in June 2024 that US finasteride prescriptions for men aged 25 and over had risen nearly 200 percent over seven years, per Epic Research, and that doctors saw more patients starting in their late teens. It credited telehealth companies such as Hims, Keeps and Ro, social media influencers and the r/tressless community with promoting the drug.[13]

On looksmax.org, minoxidil threads cover beard, eyebrow and scalp use, application questions and alternatives. One user asked about alternatives to minoxidil, and a reply said hair would return to baseline thickness rather than fall out if he stopped; another 15-year-old asked about using minoxidil on eyebrows twice a day and was told by a reply that there is no age requirement, an exchange that illustrates how off-label use is discussed informally.[17][18] Wikipedia notes minoxidil has been studied off-label for beard growth, including in transgender men.[3]

Telehealth marketing and influencer promotion have drawn regulatory attention in the UK.[15] Dermatologists quoted by NBC say the drug is prescribed constantly and that long-term data are limited but suggest benefits persist.[13][15]

Wikipedia lists a combination of finasteride, latanoprost and minoxidil (TH-07) in phase 2 as of December 2023, and extended-release oral and sublingual minoxidil in phase 3 as of September 2025.[3] A registered phase 3 trial of TH07 (NCT07435012) is recruiting 420 participants.[19] Topical finasteride, per Wikipedia, has preliminary research suggesting benefit in pattern hair loss along with lower serum DHT.[4]

lore.intro: Fin+min is discussed on looksmax.org and in hair-loss communities such as r/tressless as the basic treatment against hair loss, with debate over adding oral minoxidil or dutasteride and over avoiding finasteride because of side-effect fears.[13][17]

claims.claim: Finasteride plus minoxidil is the standard base for keeping hair.
claims.believers: Users and clinicians describe the pair as the default, with finasteride slowing loss and minoxidil adding regrowth, and say starting early gives the best result.[13]
claims.experts: Both drugs outperformed placebo in randomised trials and are FDA-approved for the condition; combination-specific trials are small.[2][10][11]

claims.claim: Finasteride can cause lasting sexual problems or post-finasteride syndrome.
claims.believers: Affected users and advocacy groups such as the PFS Foundation report persistent sexual, mood and cognitive symptoms after stopping.[15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports an FDA label update on persistent sexual effects, a 2019 BMJ editorial calling the syndrome ill defined, and a meta-analysis finding associations with limited evidence quality.[4]

claims.claim: Finasteride causes depression and suicidal thoughts.
claims.believers: Users and some researchers cited by the BBC argue the drug raises depression risk.[15]
claims.experts: In May 2025 the EMA confirmed suicidal ideation as a side effect of finasteride, frequency unknown, while concluding benefits outweigh risks for approved uses.[14]

claims.claim: Topical finasteride gets the benefit with fewer side effects.
claims.believers: Some users prefer topical mixtures to limit exposure through the bloodstream.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says topical finasteride also lowers serum DHT, and the EMA found no evidence linking skin sprays to suicidal ideation; a small Indian study reported maintained density on a topical combination.[4][14][8]

claims.claim: Oral minoxidil works better than topical minoxidil.
claims.believers: Users who dislike greasy solutions or scalp irritation turn to tablets and report thicker hair.
claims.experts: A 2024 randomised trial found oral minoxidil did not demonstrate superiority over twice-daily 5% topical, with more hypertrichosis in the oral group; a 2022 review reported oral minoxidil outperforming topical.[6][5]

claims.claim: Stopping minoxidil makes your hair fall out or leaves you worse off.
claims.believers: Forum replies say hair would simply return to baseline thickness rather than fall out.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports the effects are reversible and that density returns to placebo levels about 24 weeks after stopping.[3]

claims.claim: Minoxidil also grows beards and eyebrows.
claims.believers: Forum users, including teenagers, apply minoxidil to eyebrows and beards.[18]
claims.experts: Beard growth has been studied off-label, including in transgender men, according to Wikipedia; it is FDA-approved only for scalp hair loss.[3]

card.summary: The standard hair-loss duo of minoxidil and finasteride; both approved and trial-backed, with finasteride's side effects debated.
card.note: Finasteride carries sexual and mood side-effect warnings; results last only while treatment continues.

quick.overview:
Fin+min combines minoxidil, which stimulates hair growth, with finasteride, which lowers DHT, the hormone behind male pattern hair loss. It is the base regimen most discussed in looksmaxxing hair-retention threads.

Each drug beats placebo in randomised trials and is FDA-approved; trials of the combination itself are small.
quick.mechanism: Minoxidil is a vasodilator prodrug that appears to prolong follicle growth; finasteride blocks type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, lowering scalp and serum DHT and slowing follicle miniaturisation.
quick.risks: Finasteride is linked to reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, mood effects and, in 2025, EMA-confirmed suicidal thoughts; persistence after stopping is disputed. Minoxidil can cause scalp irritation and, orally, fluid retention and heart effects. Benefits fade when treatment stops.
